name: Zane Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zane, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say publicly and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm a numbers man, so if you want figures, I've got figures.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good, I'll take them. What's a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a general hand and carpenter for a commercial contractor. We build the big sheds: warehouses, a supermarket last year, now a parcel depot out by the motorway junction. I do the temporary works, so site hoardings, edge protection, walkways, the timber bits nobody notices, and I've got my scaffolding ticket so I'm up on the tower scaffolds half the time. I like being high up on a clear morning when you can see the whole site. What wears me out is the wind, and the paperwork, every job's got a permit now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ania works at a dental practice on reception. Kuba's fifteen and taller than me, Zosia's eleven. We've got about four months of money in the account, and I know because I've got a spreadsheet. Our fixed mortgage rate runs out in the summer of 2028, which I think about more than I should. I use a chatbot now and then, Kuba set it up. I used it to compare mortgage deals and to write a complaint to the energy company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, another fad. Like the drones that were meant to do all our surveys and then ended up in a cupboard. I'd say it in the canteen, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd keep using the chatbot for letters and sums now and again, and work stays the same. My real worry stays the mortgage in 2028, and that's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Finish the depot, move on to whatever's next. I'd keep putting 200 a month aside for when the fix ends, so the jump in payments doesn't knock us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Boring, even. Boring's good when you've got a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drones in the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firm bought two of them three years ago. Everyone was excited, the surveyor flew them around for a month, and then the batteries kept dying in the cold and he went back to his tape and level. Last I saw, they were in a box under the site manager's desk with a coffee mug on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates. That's my monster. If our rate goes from what it is to what the bank's offering now, it's an extra 300 a month. I've done the sums three times hoping they'd change. They don't.

S0.say: There you go, another fad, like the drones that were meant to do our surveys and ended up in a cupboard. I'd say it in the canteen but I don't really post.
S0.think: For me it's fine, because work stays the same and I'd keep using the chatbot now and then for letters. My real worry is our mortgage fix ending in 2028, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.do: Finishes the parcel depot and moves to the next job. Keeps saving 200 a month toward the higher payments when the mortgage fix ends in 2028.
S0.feel: Calm, even bored, which he sees as good when there's a mortgage.
S0.quote: Last I saw, they were in a box under the site manager's desk with a coffee mug on top.
S0.fieldNote: Zane thinks in numbers and keeps a household spreadsheet. His fixation is the mortgage fix ending in 2028, which colours everything. He's a light AI user who is neither keen nor hostile. A plateau leaves him calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new kit: some of it's good, some of it's rubbish, and we'll find out which. I'd want the firm to be straight with us about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd look at which bits of my job a machine could do. Hoarding panels, edge protection, that's repeat work, a robot could probably do it. Scaffold inspections might go to cameras. I'd be okay for a while, but I'd want a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, maybe for the permit paperwork, since I hate it and it eats an hour a day. I'd watch what the firm brings in and get on the training once a couple of the lads have tried it. I'd bump savings to 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear the wind picking up while you're on the top lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a couple of the lads first. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. Remember the drones. I'm not against new things, I just don't want to waste my evenings on something that ends up under a desk. When it's proven, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about spending, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much yet. Maybe I'd hold off on the new van I've been eyeing. I'd rather have the money sitting there than on the drive.

S1.say: It's like any new kit: some good, some rubbish, and we'll find out which. I'd want the firm to be straight with us about what's coming.
S1.think: Hoarding panels and edge protection are repeat work a robot could probably do, and scaffold inspections might go to cameras. I'd be okay for a while, but I'd want a plan.
S1.do: Starts using AI tools for the permit paperwork that eats an hour a day, and joins the firm's training once a couple of workmates have tried it. Raises savings to 250 a month and holds off on buying a new van.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing the wind pick up while working on the top level of a scaffold.
S1.quote: I'm not against new things, I just don't want to waste my evenings on something that ends up under a desk.
S1.fieldNote: Zane goes through his own job task by task, which says a lot about how he thinks. He's willing to change once something is proven, and the drone story is his warning. He would put off a big purchase rather than cut everyday spending. He wants honesty from his employer more than protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, nobody planned for this, so now everyone has to. The government, the firms, all of them need to sit down and work out how people pay their bills. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 is the exact year our mortgage fix runs out. So I'd be facing a jump in payments right as my job disappears. That's the worst timing I can think of, and I've thought about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cut everything that isn't essential: Kuba's football trip, the takeaways, the streaming. Push savings hard, aim for eight months before the fix ends. I'd talk to the bank early about a longer mortgage term to lower payments. And I'd look for any job that'll last longer, maybe maintenance at the depot I'm building, since someone's got to fix the robots for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up doing the sums at two in the morning, which Ania hates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ania at two in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got it under control, which wouldn't be true. She'd know. She'd tell me to come back to bed and we'd do it on Saturday with a coffee. She's better at not panicking than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maintenance at the depot. How sure are you that job would exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. It's a guess. Somebody has to keep the robots running, but if AI can do almost anything, maybe the robots fix each other. I'd still try, because a guess is better than sitting at home.

S2.say: Nobody planned for this, so now everyone has to. The government and the firms need to sit down and work out how people pay their bills, and I'd sign things even if I'm not one for marches.
S2.think: 2028 is the exact year our mortgage fix runs out, so payments would jump just as my job disappears. That's the worst timing I can think of.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essentials straight away, including his son's football trip, takeaways and streaming, and pushes savings toward eight months. Talks to the bank early about a longer mortgage term and looks for longer-lasting work, such as maintenance at the parcel depot he's building.
S2.feel: Alarmed, up at two in the morning doing the sums.
S2.quote: 2028 is the exact year our mortgage fix runs out. So I'd be facing a jump in payments right as my job disappears.
S2.fieldNote: The clash with his mortgage date makes this picture personal for Zane. He responds with numbers and lists but admits he'd be lying to his wife if he said it was under control. He sees his next job as a guess, not a plan. His politics stay moderate: signing petitions, not marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to sort out a proper plan, if people stop arguing and get on with it. I'd say it to the lads, maybe at the parents' evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can get past the mortgage cliff in 2028 while I'm still earning. That changes a lot for me. After that, it's still the end of this kind of work, but I'd have room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep saving 250 a month and get the new mortgage locked in for as long as possible before things change. I'd look at a course in building maintenance or robot servicing, once I've seen a couple of people come out the other side with jobs. And I'd keep using the AI tools at work to get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. More like a deadline than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait for a couple of people. Who do you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law Piotr, he's an electrician and always first to try things. And the site engineer, Jade, who's young and knows all the kit. If those two say it's worth it, it usually is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different for Kuba in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be twenty when it lands. That's a scary age for it. I'd sit him down and say, do something where you can move sideways, not something narrow. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd hear me.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for a proper plan if people stop arguing and get on with it. I'd say that to the lads and maybe at parents' evening.
S3.think: Five years means I get past the mortgage cliff in 2028 while I'm still earning, and that changes a lot. It's still the end of this kind of work, but I'd have room.
S3.do: Keeps saving 250 a month and locks in a long new mortgage deal before things change. Looks at a building maintenance or robot servicing course once trusted people have done it and found jobs, and uses AI tools to work faster.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, more like a deadline than a cliff.
S3.quote: More like a deadline than a cliff.
S3.fieldNote: The key difference for Zane is clearing his 2028 mortgage reset while still earning. He follows a couple of trusted early adopters, his brother-in-law and the site engineer. His worry shifts to his eldest son, who would be twenty at the point of change. His approach stays steady and number-driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say that's time to do it properly. Retrain people, change the schools, sort the money out. I'd say it and probably vote for whoever had the most sensible-sounding plan, not the loudest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be 53. Mortgage would be well past the scary bit. Kids grown. I'd have time to move into something else gradually, maybe facilities management or inspecting. It's still an ending, but it's a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and overpay the mortgage a bit. I'd do a part-time course in building services or facilities over two or three years, after I've seen what's actually in demand. And I'd sit down with Kuba and Zosia about their plans, because they'd be the ones really living in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a worry, but it's a long way off and I've got time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Zosia's plans look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet this month, a pop star last month. I'd say great, whatever you pick, learn how the machines work alongside it. And I'd start a small savings pot for her and Kuba, maybe 30 a month each, for whatever training they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the longer warning change how you feel about the 2028 one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes the 2028 one look even worse. With ten years, I can see a path. With two, I'm just staring at a spreadsheet hoping a number changes.

S4.say: Ten years is time to do it properly: retrain people, change the schools and sort the money out. I'd vote for whoever had the most sensible plan, not the loudest.
S4.think: At 53 the mortgage would be past the scary bit and the kids would be grown. I'd have time to move gradually into facilities management or inspecting, so it's an ending, but a slow one.
S4.do: Keeps saving, overpays the mortgage a little, and takes a part-time building services or facilities course over two or three years once he sees what's in demand. Starts savings pots of about 30 a month each for his children's training.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the worry far enough off that he has time to get ready.
S4.quote: With two, I'm just staring at a spreadsheet hoping a number changes.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Zane can see a path and plans a gradual move into building services. He turns to his children's futures and starts small savings pots for them. He votes for the sensible plan over the loudest, a classic centre position. The comparison with the fast picture sharpened how much the timing matters to him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because of the mortgage. What would help is the banks being made to give people breathing room, like a payment holiday or longer terms without penalties, and some kind of income support that tides you over while you retrain. Clear information too, about which jobs are actually growing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how people like me find out what's real. I hear one thing in the canteen, another on the news, another from Kuba. Somebody needs to give working people straight numbers, not scary headlines. I'd trust a number.

headlineQuote: Boring's good when you've got a mortgage.
portrait: Zane is a 43-year-old general hand and carpenter on big commercial sheds, with scaffolding skills, a wife on a dental reception desk, two children and about four months of savings tracked in a spreadsheet. He uses AI now and then and adopts new kit once it's proven. His fixed mortgage rate ends in 2028, which makes the fast AGI picture the worst timing he can imagine and leaves him alarmed. With five or ten years he can clear that reset while earning and plan a gradual move into maintenance or building services. He wants straight numbers and sensible plans, not slogans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands just as his mortgage fix ends and his payments jump.
whatWouldHelp: Banks being made to give breathing room, such as payment holidays or longer terms without penalties, income support while retraining and clear information about which jobs are growing.
